facts: The prosecutrix, a widow of 55 years of age was criminally assaulted and subjected to forcible sexual intercourse by the respondents on 10.11.1993 near her village Baadi in Gumanu Nalla District Mandi, Himachal Pradesh when she was coming back to her house after attending the marriage of the daughter of her husband's brother.
The first Information Report was submitted by her on the next date against the respondents.
She was medically examined and her torn Salwar was sent for chemical analysis.
On medical examination various injuries were found on her person.
issues: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting the respondents of the charges framed against them?
petitioner_arguments: The prosecution had failed to prove the case against the respondent No.1 beyond reasonable doubt.

The absence of dead or alive spermatozoa either in the vagina or in the cervix of the prosecutrix rules out the possibility of the prosecutrix having been subjected to sexual intercourse on the date and time alleged by the prosecution.
respondent_arguments: The identity of respondent No.2 was not established during the investigation.
There was no unimpeachable, reliable and satisfactory evidence produced regarding his involvement in the commission of the crime.
court_reasoning: The absence of Test Identification may not be fatal if the accused is known or sufficiently described in the complaint leaving no doubt in the mind of the Court regarding his involvement.
Identification Parade may also not be necessary in a case where the accused persons are arrested at the spot.
Corroboration is admittedly only a rule of prudence.

The courts should examine the broader probabilities of a case and not get swayed by minor contradictions of insignificant discrepancies in the statement of the prosecutrix, which are not of a fatal nature, to throw out an otherwise reliable prosecution case.
holding: We agree with the finding of the High Court that accused Diwan Chand could not be held guilty as no unimpeachable, reliable and satisfactory evidence was produced regarding his involvement in the commission of the crime.

However, we are of the opinion that the High Court was not justified in holding that the prosecutrix had not been subjected to forcible sexual intercourse or the prosecution had failed to prove the case against the respondent No.1 also.
